title: Page Load Order and Long Tasks
body:
## 1. Is CSS downloaded before JavaScript?

**Answer**: not strictly "one before the other". More accurately — **they download in parallel, but they block different things, and where you put the tags is a performance convention.**

### How the browser treats the two

The browser parses HTML top to bottom and starts a download when it meets a `<link>` (CSS) or `<script>` (JS) tag. **Modern browsers do not wait for CSS to finish before starting JavaScript**; each request fires as soon as its tag is parsed, and **several requests proceed in parallel** (bounded by the per-domain connection limit, but not queued one at a time).

### What actually creates the impression of an order is where the tags sit, and each has its own reason

**CSS goes in `<head>` so it starts downloading as early as possible.** The reason: CSS is **render-blocking**. Until the CSS is downloaded and parsed, the browser **will not display the DOM it has already parsed**, because it does not want to show an ugly unstyled page and then snap the styles on — the flash of unstyled content. So the sooner CSS starts, the shorter that block.

**JavaScript goes at the bottom of `<body>` (or carries `defer`/`async`).** The reason: a plain `<script>` tag **blocks HTML parsing**. When the browser reaches a `<script>` without `defer` or `async`, it **stops parsing, downloads and executes that JavaScript**, and only then continues. Hence the bottom placement, or:

- **`defer`**: downloads without blocking parsing, then executes in order after parsing finishes
- **`async`**: downloads without blocking parsing and executes the moment it arrives; order is not guaranteed

### In one sentence

> It is not that CSS necessarily downloads before JavaScript. Both can download in parallel; CSS goes first to release render-blocking as soon as possible, and JavaScript goes last (or gets `defer`/`async`) so it does not block parsing. Render-blocking and parse-blocking are two different mechanisms, and the tag order is a performance convention, not a browser-enforced download order.

---

## 2. Understanding long tasks

### The definition

**A stretch of JavaScript that runs on the main thread for more than 50 milliseconds without being interrupted is a long task.**

### Why 50 milliseconds

People start to perceive lag at around 100 milliseconds (a rule of thumb from early usability research), and handling a user input event — a click — takes the browser some time in itself. To keep the whole chain from input to visible response under 100ms, **a single task that holds the main thread for more than 50ms is a serious risk of pushing the next interaction outside that comfortable window.** Hence 50ms as the line.

### Why long tasks are a problem

JavaScript is single-threaded; the main thread does one thing at a time. If a piece of code runs for 200ms without letting go — a textbook long task — **the browser cannot respond to any input for those 200ms.** Clicks and scrolls queue up and wait. This is exactly what **INP** is designed to catch: interaction response delay.

### The link to Fiber and time slicing — the same problem, two angles

Recall React 15's weak point, "a long render cannot be interrupted and the page stutters". What that really says is: React 15's own rendering work constitutes a long task.

Fiber's time slicing is precisely **cutting rendering work that would have been one long task into small pieces of a few milliseconds each, handing the main thread back to the browser in between so it can process queued input.**

**Put plainly, Fiber exists so that React's own rendering never becomes a long task.**

### Finding long tasks in a real project

Record an interaction in Chrome DevTools' **Performance panel** and the timeline shows red bars labelled "Long Task". It is the most direct tool for finding out why a page stutters or feels unresponsive, and clicking one shows exactly which function call took the time.

---

## Everything in one sentence

> CSS and JavaScript load in parallel; the placement of the tags addresses two different mechanisms — render-blocking for CSS, parse-blocking for JavaScript. A long task is the main thread being occupied for more than 50ms, which is the technical definition of a stuttering page, and Fiber's time slicing exists so React's own rendering never becomes one. The two topics are the resource-loading and the JavaScript-execution sides of performance work.
